open-question.question: The mission re-evaluates every one of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` and compresses each to its rule, its reason, and the retired forms that must not return. May a re-evaluation end in a rule itself being dropped or changed, for example one found obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, or does the mission change only wording and placement, every rule standing exactly as it binds today?
open-question.alternative: No rule is dropped or changed: every one of the 35 invariants keeps binding exactly as it does today. Re-evaluation cuts only text that binds nothing (mechanics already stated in the runtime files, field measurements, dates, the history of how a form came about) and moves each rule to its home. An entry that records an accepted limitation ("accepted as it stands", "accepted as never to be changed") stays as a rule, compressed to what must not be changed and why. Candidates for retirement are not recorded anywhere. The mission's diff can be reviewed as a pure move and compression: no tool, test, runtime file, or behaviour changes, and a reviewer has only to check that every rule survives, so the risk of losing a design decision while rewriting 145,667 bytes is the lowest of any option. Rules whose subject no longer stands in the tree (the pre-split missions, the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note) and entries kept only to stop a limitation being "fixed" are carried into the new tree as they are, so part of the bulk the byte budgets must hold is text the re-evaluation already judged dead, and the goal's "every invariant is re-evaluated" yields nothing beyond compression.

alternative.id: Wording only, candidates kept for later

open-question.alternative: This mission changes only wording and placement, every rule binding as it does today, as in the wording-only option. Where re-evaluation finds a rule obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, the runner leaves the rule standing in its new home and records it as a retirement candidate, with the reason, in one draft under ideas/ for a later mission to decide. Keeps this mission's diff a pure move and compression while not wasting the judgment the re-evaluation forms: the candidates reach a later mission as a ready list, where each drop can be decided on its own with the tree already in place. The dead text still has to fit inside this mission's byte budgets, and the draft is one more document the tree must point at and the update skill must keep honest until a later mission takes it up, which nothing schedules.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, and only when its subject no longer exists in the tree or the history it guards is closed (for example the pre-split missions and the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note); every other rule, accepted-limitation entries included, keeps binding exactly as today. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, the review pass authoring one open question per candidate, so the recorded decisions list every rule that leaves. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes the clearest dead weight from the tree while every drop is a recorded, revertible decision rather than a runner's call, and the rule that stops a limitation being "fixed" is left untouched, so no behaviour can drift. Adds a round of questions before derivation for a handful of small drops, and an obsolete-looking rule may still bind something (the TASKS_DONE.md note also says no runner is to read or recreate the file), so each candidate needs care that a compressed retired-forms line could have given at no cost.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete and limitation rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, when it is obsolete or when it only records an accepted limitation (the commit tool's exit-128 retry accepted as it stands, the hand-rendered attribute rule, markup accepted in an alternative's text, the unbounded show print); a dropped limitation entry leaves behaviour as it is and stops forbidding a later fix. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per candidate. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Cuts the largest class of text that binds no current behaviour, the accepted-limitation records written in the latest mission's tasks, so the tree states what the code must do rather than every fix that was weighed and declined. An accepted-limitation entry exists precisely so a later editor does not "fix" what was left on purpose; dropping it removes that guard, and a later mission may re-measure and re-decide something already settled, at a cost the drop saved only in bytes.

A rule may be dropped, never changed, when its subject no longer exists in the tree, under one criterion recorded as a decision of this mission; the task runner compressing that area applies it and names each dropped rule, with its reason, in its task's verified bar. Accepted-limitation entries and every other rule keep binding as today. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes dead rules without a question round before derivation, since applying one narrow, checkable criterion (the subject is gone from the tree) is a runner's job, and every drop still shows in a commit body and its diff. A design decision leaves the project's record by a runner's judgment rather than a recorded answer, and a runner reading "subject gone" loosely can drop a rule that still binds (a retired form that must not return is exactly a rule whose subject is gone); how much is left to runners also depends on the axis the Placement decision timing question owns.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules, docs only

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop a rule (obsolete or limitation-only) or change what it binds, narrowing, loosening, or merging rules where it finds one wrong or redundant, but only where the change needs no edit to a runtime file, tool, test, or build: the rules change what a later editor may do, never what the code does now. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Gives the re-evaluation its full value at the level of the rules themselves, so overlapping or contradictory invariants written over many missions can be reconciled into a smaller, coherent set rather than faithfully compressed, while the plugin's behaviour stays exactly as shipped. Many questions may be raised across 35 rules before derivation, lengthening the mission's preparation, and a rule changed without touching the code it governs can leave code that the new rule no longer explains or that now contradicts it until a later mission aligns them.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules with the code

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop or change any rule, and a changed rule carries the change to the runtime files, tools, tests, and rebuilt host trees it governs in this mission, so rule and code stay in step. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Every rule in the new tree states exactly what the code does, with no rule left wrong or out of step, and a defect the re-evaluation exposes is fixed where it is found rather than deferred. Turns a documentation mission into a plugin-behaviour mission of unbounded size across all of core/ and the host trees, overlapping the defined mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/ that changes the context-reading runners and finish, and mixes behaviour changes into a diff that is otherwise reviewable as moves and compression.

open-question.question: The mission's pytest check must find every pointer in the root `CLAUDE.md` and in each `README.md` node below it and prove that it resolves, and the eighteen places where today's invariants refer to one another by name become references between nodes. In what written form does a node point at another node, a file, or a place inside one, so that the check can tell a pointer from ordinary prose and resolve it: a relative Markdown link, a backticked repo-relative path, or a fixed list form of its own?
open-question.recommendation: A pointer is then one unambiguous line match that placeholders, globs, and retired file names in prose can never trip, its when-to-follow note is a delimited field the note budget measures exactly, where a link form leaves the note of an inline reference undefined, and its backticked repo-relative path is the form today's file uses and one an agent passes straight to its file tools from any node.
open-question.alternative: A pointer is a line of one fixed form of the project's own, for example `- → `docs/workflow.md#heading` — when-to-follow note`, with a backticked repo-relative path and an optional heading-slug anchor; pointers stand only on such lines, a node's pointers to what lies below it in a list of them and a cross-reference from one rule to another as such a line beneath the rule. Every other mention of a file, in backticks or a Markdown link, is ordinary prose the check does not resolve. The check is a single unambiguous line match, nothing in ordinary prose (placeholders, globs, retired file names) can trip it, and the when-to-follow note is a delimited field the note budget can measure exactly. A syntax of the project's own that no renderer makes clickable and every author must learn, cross-references cannot sit inside a rule's sentence, and every file named in prose outside those lines stays unchecked and can go stale unseen.

A pointer is a relative Markdown link, `[text](path)`, its path relative to the file that holds it, and every such link to a local target outside a code span or fenced block is a pointer the check must resolve, external URLs left alone. It names a file or folder only, never a place inside one: a reference to one rule points at the node holding it and names the rule in the link text or in prose. The when-to-follow note is the text standing after the link on its line. The simplest check that still renders as a clickable link on GitHub and in editors: it parses one standard syntax, resolves a path against the linking file, and tests that it exists, with no heading parsing, so rewording a heading can never break a pointer. The eighteen cross-references between rules land only on a whole node, leaving the reader to search it for the rule, so the question's "a place inside one" goes unresolved; the link syntax costs bytes against the byte budgets; and a file-relative path must be rewritten in every link when the node holding it moves.

A pointer is a relative Markdown link, `[text](path)` or `[text](path#anchor)`, its path relative to the file that holds it, and every such link to a local target outside a code span or fenced block is a pointer the check must resolve, external URLs left alone. A place inside a file is named by the GitHub slug of one of its headings, and the check resolves the anchor by slugging the target file's headings the way GitHub does. The when-to-follow note is the text standing after the link on its line. It is the form the repository already uses (`CONTRIBUTING.md` links `CLAUDE.md#invariants-to-preserve-when-editing-skills`, `docs/skill-reference.md` links `workflow.md#how-skills-commit`), renders clickable on GitHub and in editors, and lets a cross-reference land on the exact rule, with a renamed heading caught by the check rather than left dangling. The check must reproduce GitHub's slug rule (lower-casing, punctuation dropping, numbered suffixes for repeated headings), and an anchor exists only for a heading, so a rule written as a bullet rather than under a heading of its own cannot be pointed at; whether rules get headings is the Node structure question's to settle. File-relative paths break when the linking node moves, and the syntax costs bytes against the budgets.

A pointer is a Markdown link whose path is repo-root-relative with a leading slash, `[text](/core/tools/commit.py)` or `[text](/docs/workflow.md#anchor)`, and every such link to a local target outside a code span or fenced block is a pointer the check must resolve, external URLs left alone. A place inside a file is named by the GitHub slug of one of its headings, resolved by slugging the target's headings. The when-to-follow note is the text standing after the link on its line. The same target reads the same text in every node and matches the repo-relative paths the agents already pass to their file tools, so a node can move without its outgoing links changing, while GitHub still renders the link as clickable. A leading-slash link is a less common form whose resolution depends on the renderer (GitHub and VS Code take it from the repository or workspace root, a plain Markdown viewer from the filesystem root), and it carries the heading-anchor drawbacks: GitHub's slug rule reproduced in the check, and no anchor for a rule that has no heading of its own, the Node structure question's to settle.

A pointer is a relative Markdown link, `[text](path)` or `[text](path#id)`, its path relative to the file that holds it, and every such link to a local target outside a code span or fenced block is a pointer the check must resolve, external URLs left alone. A place inside a file is named by an explicit id the target declares in one fixed form, for example an HTML anchor `` at the rule, and the check resolves an anchor against the declared ids only, never against heading text. The when-to-follow note is the text standing after the link on its line. A cross-reference names the rule by a stable id that survives rewording or moving the rule's heading, and any rule can carry one, a bullet as well as a heading, so the eighteen by-name references ("see the committing invariant") map one-to-one onto ids with no slug rule to reproduce. Every rule pointed at carries extra markup that renders as nothing and costs bytes against the node budget, an id is one more thing an author must remember to declare, and file-relative paths still break when the linking node moves.

A pointer is a backticked repo-relative path, `core/tools/commit.py` or `docs/workflow.md#heading`, a place inside a file named by a heading slug after `#`, and every code span in path form in the root and the nodes is a pointer the check must resolve. Code spans that are not paths are told apart by a stated rule, for example one holding `<`, `*`, `{`, or a space being ordinary text. The when-to-follow note is the text standing after the path on its line. It is how today's `CLAUDE.md` already names files, the most compact form against the byte budgets, and the same text in every node, which an agent can pass straight to its file tools; every file a node mentions is checked, so no mention can rot unseen. Backticks already carry commands, placeholders (`<scope>/mission_<slug>/`, `hosts/<host>/`), globs, and the names of retired files that must not return (`TASKS_DONE.md`, `report-procedure.md`), which do not exist and would fail the check, so the exclusion rule must be drawn and kept right or authors stop naming retired forms in backticks; nothing renders as a link.

Two forms. A node's pointers to the nodes and files below it, each with its when-to-follow note, stand as lines of one fixed form of the project's own (for example `- `path` — note`, a backticked repo-relative path), which the check matches and whose note it measures. A cross-reference inside a rule's text, the eighteen by-name references among them, is a relative Markdown link with a heading-slug anchor, every local link outside a code span or fenced block resolved by the check. Bare backticked paths in prose are ordinary text the check does not resolve. Each pointer kind gets the form that fits it: the tree's structural pointers carry their note in a delimited field the note budget measures exactly, while cross-references stay inline in the rule's sentence and clickable, and placeholders and retired file names in backticks never trip the check. Two pointer forms for authors to learn and the check to parse, with the anchor drawbacks of the heading-slug form (GitHub's slug rule reproduced, no anchor for a rule without a heading, the Node structure question's to settle), and file names written as bare backticked paths in prose stay unchecked.

open-question.question: The mission's pytest check requires every covered folder to have a node, a `README.md` of its own or, where that name is taken or rendered, a description in its parent node. The repository tracks thirteen top-level folders, some holding one file (`.claude-plugin/`, `snippets/`), with subfolders below them such as `core/skills/<name>/`, `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, `tests/fixtures/`, and `gurita-vscode/src/`, beside the transient `mission_<slug>/` directories, the fixture trees, and the build output under `hosts/`. By what rule does a folder count as covered: every tracked top-level folder only, every tracked folder at any depth, every folder meeting a stated test such as a file count, or an explicit list kept by hand?

recommendation.option: Top level plus linked deeper nodes

open-question.recommendation: It checks what the goal names, a node or a root description for every top-level folder, forces no near-empty node on a one-file subfolder, and still guarantees that every deeper node someone chose to write is reachable from the root, so no node is orphaned and no depth cut-off, file-count threshold, or hand-kept list has to be tuned.

alternative.id: Top level plus linked deeper nodes

open-question.alternative: Every tracked top-level folder, with root `mission_*/` directories left out, must be covered as in the top-level rule. Below the top level no folder is required to have a node. Any `README.md` node that does stand deeper in the tree must be pointed at from its parent folder's node, or from the nearest ancestor node where the parent has none, so a deeper node exists only by choice but is never orphaned. Deeper nodes are written only where someone judged them worth writing, so the check forces no near-empty node on a one-file folder. Every node that exists can still be reached from the root, which is what a reader following pointers needs. Coverage below the top level is still opt-in: a new subfolder holding important rules gets no node unless someone writes one. The reachability check also needs a list of which `README.md` files are nodes and which are not, since the root landing page, `gurita-vscode/README.md`, and the host templates under `scripts/hosts/<host>/` are not nodes. How that is told depends on the pointer form the sibling question chooses.

A folder counts as covered exactly when it is a tracked top-level folder, read from `git ls-files`, the live `mission_*/` directories at the root left out by their name pattern: the thirteen folders today. Each must have its own `README.md` node or, where the name is taken or rendered (`core/`, `hosts/`, `gurita-vscode/`), a description in the root. No folder below the top level is checked, whether or not it holds a node. It is the smallest rule the check can state, with no exclusion list and no threshold. It matches the goal's one pointer per top-level folder, and the set changes only when a top-level folder is added or removed, so an ordinary commit deeper in the tree never makes the check fail. The check promises nothing about the subfolders where most of the rules apply, such as `core/tools/`, `core/skills/<name>/`, `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, `tests/fixtures/`, and `gurita-vscode/src/`. Whether those are described depends on each top-level node's own prose, and a node written below the top level can be left unlinked or go stale without the check noticing.

A folder counts as covered when it is tracked and lies at most two levels deep: the top-level folders and their direct subfolders, such as `core/{agents,shared,skills,tools}/`, `scripts/hosts/`, `tests/fixtures/`, `gurita-vscode/{media,runner_tests,scripts,src}/`, `.github/{ISSUE_TEMPLATE,workflows}/`, and `.claude/skills/`. The `mission_*/` directories are left out at any depth, and so is everything under `hosts/`, the build output. A covered folder whose `README.md` name is taken or rendered, which covers everything under `core/` and anything packaged from `gurita-vscode/media/`, is described in its nearest ancestor node instead. It reaches the second level, where most of the rules apply (`core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `scripts/hosts/`, `tests/fixtures/`), with a rule that fits in one line. The covered set changes only when a folder is added at one of those two levels. The cut-off is arbitrary. `core/skills/<name>/`, `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, and `gurita-vscode/src/webview/` are left out while `.claude-plugin/` and `snippets/`, one file each, are in. Everything under `core/` is rendered, so all four of its subfolders fall back to the root's description, which spends the root's byte budget.

Every tracked folder at any depth counts as covered unless it falls under a fixed set of exclusion patterns written in the check: `hosts/**` (build output published verbatim), `mission_*/` at any depth (a mission directory holds exactly its three files), and `tests/fixtures/**` (fixture trees seeded or parsed by tests). Every remaining folder needs its own `README.md` node, or a description in its nearest ancestor node where the name is taken or rendered. That fallback covers every folder under `core/`, every folder under `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, where a file would be rendered into the host tree, and `gurita-vscode/media/`, whose files are packaged. Nothing escapes the check. A new folder anywhere outside the excluded areas fails the check until it is described, so the tree cannot fall behind the repository in the way the old layout block fell behind `ideas/`. Today it covers roughly 70 folders, among them each of the 22 `core/skills/<name>/` directories and each `scripts/hosts/<host>/` subfolder down to `plugins/gurita/.codex-plugin/`. Many of those can only be described in an ancestor, so the description lines pile up in the root and the `scripts/hosts/` node, which strains the byte budgets the sibling question sets. The exclusion patterns also become one more rule that must be kept in step with the tree.

A tracked folder outside the excluded areas (`hosts/**`, `mission_*/` at any depth, `tests/fixtures/**`) counts as covered when it is top-level or when it directly holds at least a stated number of tracked files, the number written in the check. A covered folder whose `README.md` name is taken or rendered is described in its nearest ancestor node instead. Nodes are required where a folder holds enough files to need explaining, while one-file subfolders and single-skill directories need none. The cost scales with how much a folder holds rather than with how deep it sits. Whether a folder is covered changes as files come and go. A commit that adds one file to an unrelated folder can push it over the threshold and make the check fail at a moment that has nothing to do with documentation. The threshold itself is a number with no principled value, and it treats a small folder full of rules, such as `core/tools/` with its six tools, the same as one holding fixtures.

A folder counts as covered exactly when it appears on an explicit list kept by hand in one tracked place, in the check itself or in a file it reads. The list names the top-level folders as well as any deeper ones. The check proves that every listed path exists as a tracked folder and has a node or a parent description, and it checks nothing about unlisted folders. The maintainer decides folder by folder where a node is worth having, with no exclusion patterns or thresholds to tune. Folders whose name is taken or rendered are simply listed with their fallback, and a stale entry for a folder that no longer exists fails the check. A new folder, even at the top level, escapes the check silently until someone adds it to the list. The list itself becomes another inventory of the tree kept by hand, which is how the old layout block drifted. Keeping it current falls to the update skill, whose job the sibling question decides.

alternative.id: Top level plus listed deeper folders

open-question.alternative: Every tracked top-level folder, with root `mission_*/` directories left out, is covered by rule, so a new top-level folder fails the check until it is described. Deeper folders are covered only when they appear on a hand-kept list in one tracked place, such as `core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `scripts/hosts/`, and `tests/fixtures/`. Each listed folder needs a node or a description in its nearest ancestor node, and each listed path must exist. Nothing new escapes at the top level, and deeper coverage goes exactly where the maintainer judges the rules apply, with no depth cut-off or file-count threshold deciding for them. It carries both mechanisms. A new subfolder holding rules is missed unless it is added to the list, and the list is an inventory kept by hand that can drift. The check has two kinds of coverage to explain, one by rule and one by listing.

open-question.question: The goal lists what the small root `CLAUDE.md` holds, among it one pointer per top-level folder, and names no place for what must be known about the files standing at the repository root, which today's layout block describes one entry each (`VERSION`, `task_line_rules.txt`, `answer_decision_principles.md`, the policy and contributor files). Where is that recorded: as entries in the root within its byte budget, in a document the root points at, only in each file's own header or in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or nowhere beyond the rules that bind everywhere?
open-question.recommendation: Every binding root file is described where a reader meets it, in the file itself or, for the few that can carry no prose, in the always-loaded root, so nothing is stated twice and the root spends bytes only on entries with no other home; two of the files already open with such a header.
open-question.alternative: Each root file that can carry prose describes itself in its own header, as in the headers-only option, and the root `CLAUDE.md` carries a short entry, inside its byte budget, only for the root files that cannot carry one and still bind work (chiefly `VERSION` and `.python-version`, with `AGENTS.md` as the symlink to the root itself); policy, licence, and lock files get no entry. Every binding root file is described somewhere a reader will meet it, either inside the file opened or in the always-loaded root, while the root spends bytes only on the few files that have no other home. Two homes follow one rule (header if possible, root otherwise) that a reader has to know to look in the right one, and a self-describing file whose header is later trimmed falls through both with nothing to notice it.

The root `CLAUDE.md` carries one short entry for every tracked file standing at the repository root (today `.gitignore`, `.python-version`, `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `LICENSE`, `README.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `VERSION`, `answer_decision_principles.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `task_line_rules.txt`, `uv.lock`), inside its byte budget, and the mission's pytest check is extended to fail when a tracked root-level file has no entry. The root is the one file every host loads, so whoever meets a root file finds its role and binding rule (for example that `VERSION` is the single source of truth written only by `set_version.py`) in the place already read, and the check keeps a new root file from going undescribed the way the `ideas/` entry silently fell behind the tree. Fourteen entries, most of them self-evident policy and lock files, spend root bytes the goal wants for the cross-cutting rules and the folder pointers, and the check gains a root-file rule beyond the three it names; whether it fits depends on the root limit the byte-budget sibling sets.

The root `CLAUDE.md` carries an entry only for the root files whose role or rule is not plain from their name and kind (such as `VERSION`, `task_line_rules.txt`, `answer_decision_principles.md`, the `AGENTS.md` symlink, and `.python-version`), inside its byte budget, chosen by judgment; the policy, licence, and lock files get none, and no check enforces which files are listed. Root bytes go only to what a reader would otherwise get wrong, keeping the facts that bind (the version's mirrors, the rule file read by the extension's runner, the principle store's sole writer) in the always-loaded file at a fraction of the cost of listing everything. Which files count as unclear is a judgment nothing checks, so a newly added root file can go undescribed unnoticed, the same drift that let the earlier hand compression and the layout block fall out of step with the tree; its room still depends on the root limit the byte-budget sibling sets.

The descriptions of the root files go into one new document of their own, standing at the root beside them (the root `README.md` name being taken by the landing page), and the root `CLAUDE.md` carries one pointer with a when-to-follow note to it, as it does for each top-level folder; the document is held to the node byte budget and its pointer checked like any other. Every root file can be described fully, with its reason and retired forms, without spending the root's budget, and the descriptions sit in one predictable place reached by the same pointer mechanism the rest of the tree uses. It adds a new root-level file, itself one more thing at the root to describe, and puts one extra hop between a reader and facts as small as a one-line rule on `VERSION`; whether the check treats it as a node depends on what the covered-folder and pointer-form siblings settle.

The descriptions of the root files go into a section of the existing `CONTRIBUTING.md`, beside its `## Development` section that already holds the build loop and the version bump, and the root `CLAUDE.md` points at that section with a when-to-follow note; no new file is added. It reuses the document that already owns the repository's maintainer mechanics (the version bump, the distribution repositories) and is the natural first read for a contributor, so the root files are described where the work that touches them is already described, at no cost to the root's budget and with no new file. `CONTRIBUTING.md` is a public contributor document outside the node tree, so maintainer rules on files such as the principle store mix into it, and its size falls under no byte budget unless the check is extended to it, leaving it free to grow back the way the root once did.

Each root file that can carry prose describes itself in its own header or opening paragraph (the comment block of `task_line_rules.txt`, the introduction of `answer_decision_principles.md`, comments in `pyproject.toml`, the policy files' own text), and the files that cannot (`VERSION`, which `build_hosts.py` reads bare, `LICENSE`, `uv.lock`, `.python-version`) are described only by the docstrings of the scripts that read or write them; the root `CLAUDE.md` carries no root-file entry and no pointer for them. The description lives in the file itself or its one writer, so it changes in the same commit as the file and cannot drift apart from it, and the root spends nothing on root files; two of them, `task_line_rules.txt` and `answer_decision_principles.md`, already open with such a header. Nothing in the always-loaded root tells a reader these files carry rules, so the bare `VERSION` rule (single source of truth, mirrored by `set_version.py` alone) is found only by someone who already opens `scripts/set_version.py`, and no check confirms that any file still describes itself.

Each root file is described in the node of the folder holding the code that reads or writes it, `VERSION` with `set_version.py` and `build_hosts.py` in the `scripts/` node, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and `.python-version` with the test runs, `task_line_rules.txt` with the extension's runner, and `answer_decision_principles.md` with the runtime that reads it, wherever each of those folders is described; the root `CLAUDE.md` carries no root-file entries, and files no tracked code reads (the policy files) are described nowhere. A maintainer changing the code that handles a root file meets its rule exactly where they work, and the root's budget goes wholly to the cross-cutting rules and the folder pointers. A reader starting from the root file itself finds no pointer to its description, several files have more than one reader across folders, and `core/` and `gurita-vscode/` are described by the root, so some of these entries land back in the root anyway; it depends on how the spanning-rules sibling places a rule touching several folders.

No entry, pointer, header requirement, or section records the root files as such; the only text bearing on them is whatever the rules that bind everywhere in the root `CLAUDE.md` already say, and each file is left to its name and its existing content. It is the smallest change and the smallest root: nothing new to write, keep within a budget, or check, and most root files (the licence, the policy files, the lock file, the changelog) are self-evident by name. open-question.question: GitHub's documentation says a `README.md` in `.github/` is shown as the repository's front page ahead of the root one, which has not been checked against this repository, whose root `README.md` is the public landing page. open-question.question: The mission's pytest check holds the root `CLAUDE.md`, every `README.md` node below it, and each pointer's when-to-follow note within a byte budget, and the three limits constrain one another, since the root carries one pointer with its note for each of the thirteen tracked top-level folders beside its other contents and a node carries the pointers to what lies below it. Today's root is 171,838 bytes, and an earlier hand compression to 22,329 bytes grew back. What are the three byte limits: for the root, for a node, and for a note?
open-question.recommendation: Three plain numbers with no exception table to creep upward: the root limit sits at a size already shown to hold the whole repository's guidance in compressed form, so it is meetable with the root still describing the folders whose README name is taken, a 12,000-byte node holds a folder's compressed rules, and the check still cuts today's root by about nine tenths and holds it there by test.
open-question.alternative: Three fixed numbers, each applying uniformly: the root at most 20,000 bytes, every node at most 12,000 bytes, and every note at most 400 bytes, two or three short sentences. Notes count inside the size of the file holding them, so the root's thirteen pointers take at most about 5,200 bytes, and the root total sits just under the 22,329 bytes of the earlier hand compression, which held the same eight sections with 23 invariant bullets. The root limit is close to a size already shown to hold the whole repository's guidance in compressed form, so it is very likely meetable whatever the sibling placement questions settle, while still cutting today's 171,838-byte root by about nine tenths and holding it there by test rather than by hand. A 20,000-byte root is large enough to keep many folder-specific rules in the root rather than in the nodes where someone working there would find them, so the budget does less to push knowledge down the tree; whether 12,000 bytes suffices for the largest folders still depends on the sibling questions on node structure and covered folders.

Three fixed numbers, each applying uniformly: the root `CLAUDE.md` at most 10,000 bytes, every `README.md` node at most 6,000 bytes, and every when-to-follow note at most 200 bytes, about one line. The note limit is counted inside the root's and each node's own size, so the root's thirteen top-level pointers take at most about 2,600 bytes of note text and leave the rest for what the repo is, the rules binding everywhere, the knowledge-placement rules, the description of `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/`, and the 623-byte `## Mission Workflow` section. The limits sit well below the 22,329-byte form that grew back, so the tree cannot drift toward a large root a little at a time, and every rule has to be compressed to its rule, reason, and retired forms rather than carried over with its mechanics and history. The root also has to describe `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/`, whose names are taken, and a 6,000-byte node leaves little room in folders of many files such as `tests/` (72 files outside the fixtures) or `gurita-vscode/src/` (87), so the limits may be unmeetable depending on where the core rules live, what a node's structure requires (an entry per file, for one), and whether root-level files get entries in the root, all owned by sibling questions; a limit hit by honest content invites cutting a reason rather than moving it.

Three fixed numbers set as regression guards rather than compression targets: the root and every node at most 40,000 bytes, the size at which Claude Code warns that a large `CLAUDE.md` affects performance, and every note at most 1,000 bytes. The actual compression is left to the tasks and the update skill, the check only stopping a file from growing past the ceiling. The limits are anchored to an outside threshold rather than chosen arbitrarily, so they never force a sound rule out of the file it belongs in, and no task fails merely because honest content ran a few hundred bytes over a guessed number. A root of up to 40,000 bytes is almost twice the form that grew back, so the budget gives no pressure toward a small root and the tree could regrow to a size the goal calls replacing; the warning threshold is a host behaviour no `settings.toml` records, so it is unverified here and may change, and a note of 1,000 bytes is a paragraph, not a when-to-follow note.

The root's and each node's limit covers its own body only, the pointer lines and their notes excluded and bounded separately: the root body at most 10,000 bytes, a node body at most 8,000 bytes, and each note at most 300 bytes, so the root's total grows by at most one note's allowance per pointer as top-level folders are added, about 3,900 bytes for today's thirteen. The check finds the pointers it already resolves and subtracts them before measuring the body. It removes the coupling the question names: adding a folder or a pointer never squeezes the rules standing beside them, so the root's and each node's rule budget stays fixed however many children it points at. No total size of the root is bounded, so a project growing folders grows the root without the check noticing, and the check has to tell pointer lines from body text exactly, which depends on the pointer form a sibling question owns; the limits are harder to state and to read off a file than one size per file.

The root at most 16,000 bytes, each note at most 300 bytes, and every node at most 8,000 bytes by default, with a short table kept in the check giving a larger limit, up to 16,000 bytes, to named nodes whose folders hold many files (for example `tests/` or `gurita-vscode/src/`). Every other node takes the default. It fits the repository's uneven folders, where the largest hold over seventy files and the smallest one, without either loosening every node to the largest folder's size or forcing the largest folders to drop what someone working there needs. The exception table is the growth path the earlier compression lost to: each time a node runs over, raising or adding its exception is one line in a test, so limits can creep upward with each change; which nodes need an exception at all depends on the sibling questions on node structure and covered folders.

No numbers are fixed now: the task that writes the check sets three uniform limits from the finished tree, each at the measured size plus a fixed margin of 10 percent, the root's own size, the largest node's, and the longest note's, and records them in the check. The limits are grounded in content that has actually been compressed and placed, so none is unmeetable or so loose it does nothing, and the mutual constraint between root, node, and note is satisfied by construction. The budget follows the content instead of shaping it, so the compression has no target while it is done and the largest node or the root sets the limit for everything; the decision of how small the tree must be is moved to a runner completing a task rather than made in this mission's decisions.

No uniform node limit: the check holds one table giving the root and every node its own limit, each set at that file's size when the tree is finished plus a margin of 10 percent, and every note at most 300 bytes; a new node takes a default of 8,000 bytes until its own entry is added, and a limit is raised only by editing its entry in the table. Every file is held near the size it was compressed to, so growth in any one file, the root included, is stopped at once and any raise is a visible line in a diff that a reviewer can question. The table needs an entry per node and changes whenever one is added, removed, or legitimately grows, a hand-kept list the update skill must maintain; the limits record what the tree happened to be rather than a size anyone chose, so a file compressed poorly at the start is held at its poor size.
